---
title: "The MINTverse pipeline"
---

The emulator runs from an EIR. The first stage inverts whatever you have, a measured
prevalence or an HBR, into the EIR that would sustain it in the setting it was measured
in. The second stage takes that EIR and runs the intervention forward.

## The two stages

```{.text .diagram}
  net mix (py_only, py_pbo, py_pyrrole, py_ppf)
  pyrethroid resistance
                    │
                    │  estimint.calculate_dn0
                    ▼
                  dn0_use ─────────────┐
                                       │
  measured prevalence                  │
  Q0, phi_bednets, seasonal            │
  itn_use, irs_use                     │
                    │                  │
                    │  estimint: XGBoost (prevalence -> EIR)
                    ▼                  │
                   EIR ────────────────┤
                                       │
                                       ▼
                            12 static covariates
                    eir, dn0_use, dn0_future, Q0, phi_bednets,
                    seasonal, routine, itn_use, irs_use,
                    itn_future, irs_future, lsm
                                       │
                                       │  stateMINT: Mamba2 emulator
                                       ▼
                       prevalence[157] and cases[157]
                       14-day steps, campaign at day 3285
```

Stage one is `estimint`, three gradient-boosted trees and a curve fit. It is cheap and
deterministic, and returns the equilibrium at the decision point. It has no notion of
time.

Stage two is `stateMINT`, a sequence model taking the twelve covariates, one row
describing a setting and a campaign. It emits a 157-step trajectory for prevalence and
one for cases.

Between them sits `calculate_dn0`, a lookup against published resistance curves rather
than a fitted model. It turns a procurement decision (which nets, at what coverage) into
the single lethality number both stages consume.

## Using the pipeline

`run_scenarios` executes the diagram above. It takes a list of `Scenario` objects,
derives `dn0` from each net mix, calls the XGBoost models for the baseline EIR, applies
any mosquito-density adjustment, assembles the twelve covariates, and runs the emulator.
One row comes back per scenario, with the trajectories stored as 157-element arrays in
the `prevalence` and `cases` cells.

That is the path for almost all work. The low-level functions (`calculate_dn0`,
`load_xgb_model`, `run_xgb_model` and `Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained`) allow the
pipeline to be entered part-way. Use them when EIR is already known from an
entomological study and prevalence should not be inverted at all, when the EIR itself is
the required answer, or when you are sweeping a covariate that `Scenario` does not
expose as a field.

## What the emulator is emulating

`stateMINT` was trained on output from
[`malariasimulation`](https://mrc-ide.github.io/malariasimulation/), the individual-based
transmission model. It reproduces that simulator to within its training error, in
milliseconds rather than minutes.

The emulator approximates the simulator. The simulator approximates reality. A trajectory
from `stateMINT` is a fast answer to the question "what would `malariasimulation` have
said?", not a direct claim about a district. Every structural assumption in the simulator
is inherited wholesale, and the emulator adds an approximation error of its own on top.

## Domain limits {#where-validity-is-decided}

The emulator is only as good as the region of covariate space it saw in training, and
`estimint` is only as good as the prevalences it was fitted against. Both have limits,
and both enforce them silently.

`estimint` clamps its inputs to the calibrated domain, so that `prev_y9` is clamped to
$[0.005,\ 0.80]$ and `hbr_y9` to $[5 \times 10^{3},\ 7 \times 10^{7}]$.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Silent clamping

Nothing is raised, logged, or flagged. A prevalence of 0.92 is clamped to 0.80 before the
model sees it, and a prevalence of 0.001 is clamped to 0.005. The value that comes back
looks like every other number the model returns.

Two habits guard against this. The first is to check your inputs against the bounds
before you call. The second is to treat an implausibly flat trajectory, or an EIR that
does not change as prevalence is increased, as the signature of a clamped input rather
than a finding.
:::

Below 0.005 the prevalence-to-EIR relationship becomes near-vertical, and a vanishing
change in prevalence maps to a large change in EIR. The inversion there is unstable in a
way no amount of training data fixes. Above 0.80 the training library thins out. Settings
that hyperendemic are rare in the parameter grid the simulations were drawn from.

A scenario sitting at the edge of the domain therefore requires a sensitivity check.
Perturb the inputs and see whether the conclusion still holds.
